newsitem.title: USA: Clinton-Dole debate not likely to stir Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: Clinton-Dole debate not likely to stir Wall Street.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton and Republican challenger Bob Dole sparred for 90 minutes in their first debate of the campaign on Sunday but market analysts said they did not expect much impact on Wall Street.
"It can only have an impact if Dole would have improved his chances significantly but it doesn't appear to me that that has happened," said Hugh Johnson, market analyst at First Albany Co.
Johnson and other analysts noted that Dole has been trailing in the polls for some time.
"I would say they both did well, relatively speaking," said Robert Stovall of Stovall/Twenty-First Advisers.
Stovall said Dole did better in the debate than expected and may see his standing in the polls move up. But at the same time Dole "was unable to punch any big holes in Clinton," he added.

Stovall noted that despite Clinton's repeated statements that 10.5 million new U.S. jobs have been created during his administration and Dole's rejoinder that Americans are working harder and paying more taxes, a number of economic issues such as the North American Free Trade Agreement were not discussed at all.

Michael Metz, market strategist at Oppenheimer & Co, said the debate was not likely to influence the outcome of the November election and was likely to be ignored when the markets opened on Monday morning.

"No one really pulled a significant gaffe," Metz said. He said some television viewers watched the event as if it were an Indianapolis 500 automobile race in which an accident could happen at any moment.
Metz thought Dole showed traces of a harsh side with some of his barbs at Clinton while Johnson thought Dole showed a humorous side not usually in evidence.
Stovall noted that Clinton had the advantage of being the president and confirmed that he was a better speaker than Dole, which people generally knew already.

"The stock market is thinking about a lot of other things," Johnson summed up. He noted that the Dow Jones industrials surged 60 points Friday to within eight points of 6,000 after surprisingly weak September payroll data.
As U.S. traders arrive at their desks Monday they may be more interested in the start of a flood of corporate earnings reports for the third quarter of 1996, Johnson said.
